title: Oil Hits Five-Week High Near $91 as US-Iran Ceasefire Collapses and Hormuz Shipping Stalls
excerpt: Brent crude surged to $90.75 a barrel as the Strait of Hormuz ground to near-halt, with Yemen's Houthis threatening a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia that could further choke global energy supplies.
body:
• Brent crude hit a five-week high of $90.75 a barrel on Monday before easing to around $88.54 as Iran signalled openness to negotiations
  • Strait of Hormuz transit volumes dropped to single digits — just four vessels on Sunday — as the US conducted its ninth consecutive day of strikes against Iran
  • Yemen's Houthis announced a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, threatening to cut off another major oil exporter and opening a new front in the conflict
  • A record 1.35 billion barrels of crude oil sitting on water globally may limit further price spikes, though analysts warn the risk premium could push Brent past $91

Ceasefire Unravels, Prices Surge

Global oil prices surged to their highest level in more than a month on Monday as the escalating US-Iran conflict continued to choke crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, the world's most critical energy chokepoint.

Brent crude hit an intraday peak of $90.75 a barrel — a five-week high — before easing to around $88.54 after an Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson said negotiations with the United States could be pursued. West Texas Intermediate followed a similar pattern, touching $84 before settling near $82.

The retreat proved fragile. Iran formally withdrew from the ceasefire agreement over the weekend, and the US military announced a ninth consecutive night of strikes, saying operations would "continue degrading Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial vessels and civilian mariners transiting the Strait of Hormuz."

"West Texas Intermediate followed a similar pattern, touching $84 before settling near $82.</p> <p>The retreat proved fragile."

Hormuz Shipping Grinds to Near-Halt

The most alarming development for energy markets is the collapse in Strait of Hormuz traffic. Only four vessels made the transit on Sunday, down from eight the previous day, according to LSEG data. Before the war began in February, roughly 20 percent of global oil supplies — approximately 17 million barrels per day — flowed through the narrow waterway.

Two oil tankers operated by Greek shipping company Dynacom Tankers were struck by projectiles of unknown origin on Monday while sailing off the coast of Oman. Iran's Revolutionary Guards separately claimed that two tankers "exploded" and were immobilised attempting to take what Tehran called an unsafe southern route through the strait.

"The supply narrative has become more bearish. The anticipated recovery in shipping has effectively stalled, with Strait of Hormuz transit volumes falling to single digits."

— ANZ analysts, in a research note

Houthi Blockade Threat Escalates Risk

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis announced a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia on Monday, opening a potential new front against the US and raising the threat to global energy supplies beyond the Persian Gulf. Rystad Energy's Jorge León estimated that roughly 2.5 million barrels per day of Saudi oil exports could be at risk from the Houthi threat.

The announcement sent shockwaves through energy trading desks already on edge. "The threats of a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia by the Houthis are significant because they raise the risk of disruption to another major oil exporter," said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade.

Structural Forces Compete

Despite the geopolitical premium driving prices higher, analysts note that a fundamental oversupply of crude sits beneath the conflict-driven rally. Kpler analysts pointed to a record 1.35 billion barrels of crude oil currently on water globally as a potential cap on further price increases.

Oil prices have swung wildly since the war began — from a peak of $119 in March to a trough of $69 in early July when a brief ceasefire took hold, and now back above $88 as the conflict resumed. The pattern, according to trading analysis firm TradigNews, demonstrates that crude can travel $50 in either direction depending entirely on the geopolitical state, with the fundamental glut pulling prices down whenever the risk premium fades.

Impact on India and the Diaspora

India, which imports over 85 percent of its crude oil, is among the most exposed economies. The RBI has already been selling dollars in offshore and onshore markets to defend the rupee, which has been under pressure from the oil-driven import bill surge. For Indian-American households, higher crude prices translate directly into elevated gasoline costs, with national averages already climbing toward $4 per gallon in many states.
